⚠ CLEARANCE — the drone sweeps a circle around its current position.

• Allow the chosen radius + 5 m all around (20 m → 25 m clear).
• What matters is the height of obstacles ON THE CIRCLE, not at the centre. The first pass is LOW (12 m at a 20 m radius) — a 15 m tree is in the path.
• The run from the centre out to the circle must be clear too.
• The subject at the centre can be as tall as you like: the drone never flies over it.

⚠ Do not rely on obstacle avoidance: it is not guaranteed in automatic mode. Keep the drone in sight.

Adjust each movement within safe limits
Cautious config: moderate speeds, comfortable distances and heights. Shots still look great, with good safety margins.
How much the voice assistant announces during flight.
Only critical safety alerts (critical battery, link lost, altitude exceeded, emergency stop). Silent otherwise.
Critical alerts plus safety warnings and command confirmations (take-off, landing, RTH, low battery, VLOS). Recommended.
Everything, including minor status changes (control accepted, home confirmed, distance back within limit). For training and diagnostics.
Critical safety alerts are always spoken, even in Minimal mode.
Fly the drone by voice (say \"CineFlight\" + a command)
Configured operational altitude ceiling (AGL, above take-off). Voice alerts warn as the drone approaches it; it never commands a descent.
Operational limit only. Many ordinary Canadian operations are capped at 122 m (400 ft), but confirm the limit for your operation category and authorizations.
Configured operational limit for the horizontal distance between the drone and the pilot. Voice alerts warn as the drone approaches this limit; it never triggers Return-to-Home automatically.
This is an operational limit, not a visibility guarantee. Direct visual line of sight remains the pilot\'s responsibility and may be lost before the configured limit.
On: listening starts automatically on every flight. The first time, the app asks for microphone permission. Voice is less reliable in wind or noise: the cards (tags) remain the most reliable method.
Fast: smooth, range ~4-12 m (recommended). Precise: more range (~4-15 m), uses the GPU, a bit heavier.
Uses the drone\'s sensors (Mini 4 Pro, Mavic 4...) to brake in front of an obstacle. OFF recommended for Test 1 (follow only).
Start the video automatically when you lock a target
On: you never forget to film a shot. Off: you press REC yourself, and a \"REC OFF\" reminder shows if the drone follows without recording.
Video resolution and smoothness. Choose before taking off.
24 — The cinema look. A slight motion blur makes movement feel more natural. Ideal for calm, cinematic shots.
30 — The standard. Slightly crisper in motion and suited to most screens. The safe choice if unsure.
60 fps — Very smooth. Allows 2× slow motion to soften a drone move or follow a fast subject.
100 fps — 4× slow motion. Ideal for very slow, Apple TV-style shots, with plenty of light.
200 fps — 8× slow motion. To break down extremely fast action; usually excessive for a plain landscape.
JPEG only. Fast stitching, light files. Enough to check the horizon, the seams and the composition, or to share right away.
DNG only. Far more latitude on sky and shadows — but our server stitches from JPEGs: without them, nothing will be stitched automatically. Reserve this for desktop processing.
DNG + JPEG. The JPEG feeds the automatic stitching and the check; the DNG stays on the card to rework the best panoramas on a computer.\n\n⚠ Two files per shot: 61 photos approach 2.5 GB of card.

The file comes out at normal speed: the slowdown happens in editing, by replaying it at 24 or 30 fps. An impossible combination falls back to the nearest supported value.
The slow-landscape look does not come from frame rate alone: it relies mostly on a VERY slow, well-stabilised drone move. Flying fast at 100 fps will not produce that effect.
Long-press Rail A: the drone slides this distance toward the filmed person.
Only used for custom (advanced) follow. The « Follow a person » and « Follow a vehicle » cards do not use this list.
The change applies at the next detection start (reopen the cockpit). If Precise makes the image stutter on your phone, go back to Fast.
OFF: no sensor braking (following relies on the camera alone). ON: forced braking, to test avoidance. AUTO: braking if the drone has sensors, otherwise inactive (production mode).
Drone height during orbit. Higher = plunging view, more scenery. Lower = eye-level shot, more intimate.
Distance between the drone and you. Large radius = wide orbit, slow background, majestic. Small radius = drone close, fast background, dynamic but can feel dizzying.
Rotation speed around you. Slow = very cinematic and stable. Fast = energetic but rushed image.
Follow distance. Large = wide shot, places you in the setting. Small = tight shot, more intimate but less margin.
Height during follow. Higher = overview of the route. Lower = sense of speed and closeness.
Follows your sideways movements. High = sticks to your moves. Low = smooth, fluid follow.
Pull-back speed to reveal the scene. Slow = gradual, dramatic reveal. Fast = express unveiling.
Climb speed during the reveal. High = gain height fast, grand. Low = gentle climb.
Approach speed toward you. Slow = controlled and safe. Fast = dramatic impact, leave room.
Distance at which the drone stops as it approaches. Larger = comfortable safety margin. The 2 m minimum protects against getting too close.
Correction speed to keep you centered. High = sharp recentering but jerky image. Low = smooth, cinematic movements.
Drone height during pull-back. At eye level = immersive and frontal. Higher = slight downward angle, more ground scenery.
Drone offset angle. 0 = straight ahead. Toward left/right = slight three-quarter, more cinematic. Approximate angle (not locked): in a sharp turn it may drift, the drone doesn\'t know your direction.
Drone height during follow. At eye level = immersive. Higher = plunging rear view, shows the route ahead of you.
Drone angle behind you. 0 = straight behind you. Toward left/right = three-quarter back, more dynamic. Approximate angle (not locked).
How tightly the drone sticks when you move away. High = firm chase, stays near you. Low = loose follow, keeps distance.

Locks onto the subject, stable shot. Show it first as you take your place.

What it does: the drone recognizes you and keeps you centered in the frame, still and stable.

When to use it: right at the start, as you stand in front of the drone, before any other tag.

Tip: stand squarely facing it, a few meters away, until the screen confirms the lock.
SHOT. Face and shoulders fill the frame. Intimate, expressive.

What it does: the drone moves in so your face and shoulders fill the frame.

When to use it: for emotion, a message to camera, an expressive detail.

Tip: show this shot first, THEN a movement. Avoid pairing it with a fast movement.
SHOT. From mid-thigh to head. Balanced, versatile (default).

What it does: the drone frames you from mid-thigh to head. It's the most balanced shot.

When to use it: almost anywhere. It's the safe, versatile default.

Tip: when in doubt about framing, pick the American shot - it works with every movement.
SHOT. The whole person, head to toe. Shows posture.

What it does: the drone shows you in full, head to toe.

When to use it: to show posture, gestures, dance, or when you move around a lot.

Tip: great with Tracking or Follow, as it leaves room if you move.
SHOT. You and the whole scene. Sets the place, gives scale.

What it does: the drone pulls back to show you AND all the surroundings.

When to use it: to establish the place, give a landscape its scale, open or close a sequence.

Tip: perfect with Reveal or Lead. Avoid it with Push-in (opposite goals).
MOVEMENT. The drone stays put and keeps you framed.

What it does: the drone holds still in a hover and keeps you in the frame.

When to use it: for a calm shot, an interview, a composed presentation.

Tip: works with every shot. The simplest and steadiest way to start.
MOVEMENT. The drone circles around you. A spectacular circular shot.

What it does: the drone circles around you while keeping the lens pointed at you.

When to use it: for a spectacular reveal, a dynamic portrait, to show off a location.

Tip: stay still at the center. Pick an American or Full shot for a nice stable track.
MOVEMENT. It moves alongside you as you walk.

What it does: the drone moves to the side and travels with you as you walk.

When to use it: to follow a walk, glide along a scene, accompany a move.

Tip: walk at a steady pace. Use a Full or Wide shot, not a Close-up.
MOVEMENT. It pulls back and rises to unveil the scene.

What it does: the drone gradually backs away and climbs to unveil the scene around you.

When to use it: for a beautiful opening, to reveal a landscape, to end a sequence on a high note.

Tip: ideal with a Wide shot. Doesn't combine with a Close-up.
MOVEMENT. It moves gently closer to you.

What it does: the drone eases closer to you to tighten the focus.

When to use it: to intensify an emotion, close on a face, build tension.

Tip: excellent with the Close-up. Doesn't combine with a Wide shot.
MOVEMENT. You fly with the sticks; the camera keeps you framed.

What it does: you fly the drone with the sticks, and the camera keeps framing you.

When to use it: when you want to choose the path yourself while staying on camera.

Tip: keep your stick movements gentle for smooth footage.
MOVEMENT. It travels ahead of you as you move forward.

What it does: the drone backs away ahead of you and films you from the front as you move forward.

When to use it: for a walk toward camera, an arrival, an intro shot.

Tip: move at a steady pace. Use a Full or Wide shot, never a Close-up.
MOVEMENT. It follows you from behind, energetic and responsive.

What it does: the drone follows you from behind, energetic and responsive.

When to use it: for action, sport, following a fast move or a descent.

Tip: leave room with a Full or Wide shot to stay in frame.
Pauses the follow. The drone stays steady (hover).

What it does: pauses the follow. The drone holds still in a hover.

When to use it: to think, reposition yourself, or interrupt a movement without stopping everything.

Tip: show a new shot or movement to resume filming.
Emergency stop. Halts everything, even a macro in progress.

What it does: emergency stop. Immediately halts all movement, even a sequence in progress.

When to use it: the moment a situation worries you or you want to stop everything at once.

Tip: keep it within reach at all times during flight.
